# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm)

The first half of this comment, sections 1–4, is valuable. It uses the microdata to put numbers on problems that could only be suspected from the working paper, and most of the arithmetic checks out. The second half and the conclusion go well beyond that evidence:
- The headline claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the authors' own corrected estimate.
- It is also contradicted by the randomised evidence the comment itself cites approvingly.
- That evidence is used selectively.

## 1. Arithmetic: mostly correct, with two exceptions

These figures reconcile:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| 34.6 / 40.3 | 0.859 (−14.1%) ✓ |
| 34.8 / 40.4 | 0.861 (−13.9%) ✓ |
| 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% ✓ |
| 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% ✓ |
| 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% ✓, and below half of 23.4 ✓ |
| Real revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |
| "Six points" overstatement of hours cut (20 − 14.1) | ✓ |

Two figures do not reconcile.

**The hours decomposition doesn't add up (§3).** Four days at +0.7 hours a day is 2.8 hours, and the day-off work adds 1.6, so 4.4 hours a week above a 32-hour schedule. That implies about 36.4 hours, or about 36.6 if the +0.7 is measured against baseline daily hours of roughly 8.06. The reported figure is 34.6, which is only 2.6 hours above schedule. Possible explanations:
- the +0.7 is measured against a different reference;
- the two components come from different subsets;
- one of the figures is wrong.

This needs reconciling. If the components are right, actual hours fell even less than reported and the corrected gain would be *smaller*. So this cuts in the authors' favour, but it still needs fixing.

**The "month ten" extrapolation (§6).** Energy fell from 0.61 SD at month three to 0.29 SD at month six. That is about 0.107 SD per month. Extrapolated linearly, it reaches zero at roughly month 8.7, not month 10.

## 2. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own results

The corrections in Table 2 leave a gain of **+10.8% per actual hour** in the best-measured subset. To reach "entirely an artifact," the comment has to eliminate that residual. The only argument offered is the novelty hypothesis in §6, which rests on:
- a two-point trend in a self-reported *energy* scale, not output;
- an extrapolation that is miscalculated;
- a burden-of-proof argument rather than data.

**The authors have data that could test novelty directly.** The Halden primary outcome was reported *monthly*. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should peak early and decline across months 1–6, at least in the 17-organisation subset. The comment doesn't examine this, even though it is the obvious test of its main claim.

The Data note also says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The conclusion then generalises to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general. Those two statements are inconsistent.

## 3. The Varden trial is used selectively

The comment calls the Varden counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." But the same trial's case-processing stratum reported **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. That estimate comes from a design that meets nearly every recommendation in the comment's own §8:

| Comment's recommendation | Varden case-processing |
|---|---|
| Record-based output | ✓ case-management system |
| Actual hours | ✓ timesheets |
| Randomised comparison group | ✓ |
| Analysis not limited to survivors | ✓ (no office attrition reported) |
| Long follow-up | Partial: 9 months, with 24-month follow-up under way |

That estimate is hard to reconcile with "entirely an artifact," and the comment never mentions it. Varden's counter offices also showed +6.7% per actual hour.

There are real caveats to Varden's per-hour gains, such as utilisation effects in counters and meeting removal in case-processing. But those are arguments about *what kind* of gain it is, not arguments that no gain exists. The comment should engage with the case-processing estimate. Without that, citing only the negative stratum looks like cherry-picking.

## 4. The meetings section (§7) mischaracterises the Varden analysis

- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** The Varden paper says the calendar data were collected *in month six at managers' request*. That was before the nine-month results. Those authors also labelled the analysis unregistered, flagged the n = 7 limitation themselves, and registered a confirmatory test for 24 months. The comment's characterisation should be corrected.
- **"Fitted to a subgroup."** The seven offices are all treated case-processing offices. That is a stratum defined before randomisation, not a selected subgroup.
- **Ignored corroboration.** The comment overlooks the Halden pilot's own interviews, in which 47 of 58 managers cited cutting meetings. That is weak evidence, but it comes independently from a different setting.

There is also a logical problem. Removing low-value meeting time is a *real* source of per-hour gain, not an artifact. Dismissing it is convenient for the "entirely artifact" thesis, but the evidence warrants "unconfirmed," not "should not be cited."

A sharper critique is available and goes unmade. If meetings drive the gain, the gain might be achievable *without* reducing hours. That challenges the policy case without denying the effect exists.

## 5. Attrition (§1): a valid finding, but its impact isn't quantified

The discrepancy is serious and worth highlighting. The working paper said withdrawals occurred "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show seven of nine withdrew after the schedule began, and six cited workload or output.

However, the abstract says that correcting "the first three" problems brings the gain to 10.8%. Attrition is the first of those problems, yet Table 2 applies no attrition correction at all. The 10.8% comes from the output and hours corrections only.

The likely size of the attrition effect on the per-hour figure is also modest. Suppose the 9 withdrawn organisations were average-sized with an output index of 85. The overall mean would fall from 98.7 to about 96.9, and the per-hour gain from 23.4% to about 21%. Eliminating the gain would require the dropouts' output to be catastrophically low.

Attrition matters more for the 92% continuation rate and the sector claims than for the per-hour number. Bounds would make this concrete, for example worst-case imputation or Lee bounds, if the withdrawn organisations left any output data.

The abstract also says the four problems "account for most of the reported gain." Revenue doesn't enter the per-hour calculation at all, and attrition isn't applied. So the 54% reduction comes from two of the four problems.

## 6. The record-based output measure has its own problems

The −3.8-point gap between manager-reported and record-based output is a useful finding, and 19 of 23 in one direction is meaningful. Some qualifications:

- **"Billable hours delivered" is an input, not an output.** In an hours-reduction pilot, billable hours mechanically fall with hours. Any organisation using it as its output record will show reduced output and roughly flat per-hour productivity almost by construction. The comment should say how many of the 23 used billable hours and show results without them.
- **Narrow records.** Records may capture only part of output, such as tickets closed without regard to quality or complexity. A manager's index could legitimately reflect output that the records miss, so not all of the gap is necessarily bias.
- **Self-selected subsets.** The record, time-tracking, and overlap subsets (23, 27, 17) chose to submit records or used time tracking. The Data note acknowledges this, but the abstract and conclusion don't. Time-tracking organisations are plausibly concentrated in software and professional services, the sectors where the original pilot reported the largest gains. If so, the corrected estimate may actually be biased *upward* relative to the full sample. That should be investigated rather than assumed away.

## 7. Revenue deflator (§4)

The point is correct in direction. However, CPI is a consumer price index and isn't the right deflator for business revenue in professional services, software, and non-profit organisations. Sector output-price or producer-price indices would be more appropriate and could give a different real figure. Non-profit "revenue" such as grants and donations is also a doubtful indicator of output. The conclusion that the figure "gives a misleading impression of growth" stands either way.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Retail with records (−11.2%)** rests on 3 organisations. The resemblance to Varden's −11.4% is suggestive, but it shouldn't be presented as confirmation.
- **"The only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work"** may be true of the studies discussed, but it is a claim about the whole literature and should be sourced or hedged.
- **"In our assessment" followed by "entirely"** is hedged phrasing attached to an unhedged claim. Readers will remember the "entirely."

## Suggested reframing of the conclusion

> In the subset of organisations where correction is possible, using record-based output and actual hours reduces the implied per-hour gain from 23.4% to about 11%. Attrition after the schedule began was more substantial, and more clearly linked to workload, than the working paper reported. Whether the remaining gain persists is untested; the pilot's monthly output data could address this. Randomised evidence from Varden County finds per-hour gains of a similar size in backlog-based work, and reduced per-employee output and service in coverage-bound work. The case for reduced hours is therefore strongest where output is not tied to presence, and the reported pilot figures substantially overstate the gains.

## Priority fixes

1. Reconcile the hours decomposition in §3.
2. Correct the month-ten extrapolation.
3. Test novelty using the monthly output series.
4. Engage with Varden's case-processing result.
5. Correct the characterisation of Varden's meetings analysis.
6. Quantify or bound the attrition effect, or remove the claim that it accounts for the gain.
7. Report results excluding billable-hours measures.
8. Bring the abstract and conclusion into line with the Data note.
